Question 1: Implementing K-means

K-means is a relatively simple algorithm that we can write ourselves. For Questions 1 and 2, do not use an existing function that performs K-means directly.

Generate 10 observations with two independent standard normal coordinates. Set a random seed and report it. Randomly assign the observations to K=2K=2 clusters, making sure neither cluster is empty. Let C(i)C(i) denote the cluster assigned to observation xix_i, and let mkm_k denote the mean of cluster kk.

  1. Perform one iteration: calculate the cluster means, then assign each observation to its closest mean using Euclidean distance. Report the means and updated assignments, and plot the observations colored by their updated assignments.

  1. Write a function that repeats these two steps until the assignments stop changing or a specified maximum number of iterations is reached. Your function should work for a data matrix with any number of variables and a chosen number of clusters KK. Start from a nonempty assignment to each cluster; if a cluster becomes empty during iteration, keep its previous mean. Recalculate the cluster means from the final assignments before returning them. Return the final assignments, cluster means, and within-cluster sum of squares,

    ∑k=1K∑i:C(i)=k‖xi−mk‖2. \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i:\,C(i)=k}\lVert x_i-m_k\rVert^2. 

my_kmeans <- function(X, K, initial_assignment, max_iter = 100) {

  # Start with the initial assignments
  assignment <- initial_assignment

  # Store the number of observations and variables
  n <- nrow(X)
  p <- ncol(X)

  # Initialize means
  means <- matrix(NA, nrow = K, ncol = p)

  for (iteration in 1:max_iter) {

    # Calculate cluster means
    for (k in 1:K) {

      # If the cluster has observations, calculate its mean
      if (sum(assignment == k) > 0) {
        means[k, ] <- colMeans(
          X[assignment == k, , drop = FALSE]
        )
      }

      # If the cluster is empty, keep its previous mean
      # For the first iteration, this should not happen because
      # initial assignments are nonempty
    }

    # Create updated assignments
    new_assignment <- numeric(n)

    # Assign each observation to its closest mean
    for (i in 1:n) {

      distances <- numeric(K)

      for (k in 1:K) {
        distances[k] <- sqrt(
          sum((X[i, ] - means[k, ])^2)
        )
      }

      new_assignment[i] <- which.min(distances)
    }

    # Stop if assignments do not change
    if (all(new_assignment == assignment)) {
      assignment <- new_assignment
      break
    }

    # Otherwise, update assignments
    assignment <- new_assignment
  }


  # Recalculate means from final assignments
  for (k in 1:K) {

    if (sum(assignment == k) > 0) {
      means[k, ] <- colMeans(
        X[assignment == k, , drop = FALSE]
      )
    }
  }


  # Calculate within-cluster sum of squares
  wcss <- 0

  for (k in 1:K) {

    for (i in which(assignment == k)) {

      wcss <- wcss +
        sum((X[i, ] - means[k, ])^2)
    }
  }


  # Return results
  return(list(
    assignments = assignment,
    means = means,
    wcss = wcss,
    iterations = iteration
  ))
}

  1. For K=2,3,5,10K=2,3,5,10, apply your function to the pixel data. Report the cluster means and within-cluster sum of squares for each KK. Reconstruct and plot each compressed image by replacing every pixel with its assigned cluster mean. Use the same RGB scale for all fits.
# Question 2

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(43251)

# Convert the image into a data matrix
# Each row = one pixel
# Columns = Red, Green, Blue
pixel_data <- matrix(img, ncol = 3)

colnames(pixel_data) <- c("Red", "Green", "Blue")

# Values of K to try
K_values <- c(2, 3, 5, 10)

# Get the dimensions of the image
height <- dim(img)[1]
width <- dim(img)[2]

# Create lists to store the results
results <- list()
compressed_images <- list()


# Repeat the K-means process for each value of K
for (K in K_values) {
  
  # Create a random initial assignment
  initial_assignment <- sample(
    1:K,
    size = nrow(pixel_data),
    replace = TRUE
  )
  
  # Make sure every cluster has at least one observation
  while (length(unique(initial_assignment)) < K) {
    
    initial_assignment <- sample(
      1:K,
      size = nrow(pixel_data),
      replace = TRUE
    )
  }
  
  
  # Run your K-means function
  result <- my_kmeans(
    X = pixel_data,
    K = K,
    initial_assignment = initial_assignment,
    max_iter = 100
  )
  
  
  # Store the results
  results[[as.character(K)]] <- result
  
  
  # Print the results
  cat("\n-------------------------\n")
  cat("K =", K, "\n")
  
  cat("\nCluster means:\n")
  print(result$means)
  
  cat("\nWithin-cluster sum of squares:\n")
  print(result$wcss)
  
  
  # Replace each pixel with the mean RGB value
  # of the cluster it belongs to
  compressed_pixels <- result$means[
    result$assignments,
  ]
  
  
  # Turn the pixels back into an image
  compressed_img <- array(
    compressed_pixels,
    dim = c(height, width, 3)
  )
  
  
  # Store the compressed image
  compressed_images[[as.character(K)]] <- compressed_img
  
  
  # Plot the compressed image
  plot(
    1,
    type = "n",
    xlim = c(0, width),
    ylim = c(height, 0),
    xlab = "",
    ylab = "",
    axes = FALSE,
    main = paste("Compressed Image: K =", K)
  )
  
  rasterImage(
    compressed_img,
    0,
    height,
    width,
    0
  )
}

Question 3: Hierarchical clustering of cars

The file data/mtcars.csv contains 11 numerical variables for 32 cars, including fuel economy, horsepower, and weight. The car column gives the model names; use it to label observations, not as a clustering variable. You may use existing hierarchical clustering functions for this question.

  1. Standardize each numerical variable to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Using Euclidean distance, perform hierarchical clustering with single, complete, and average linkage. Plot the three dendrograms with the car names and compare the results.

# Save car names
car_names <- mtcars$car

# Remove the car column
# Keep only the 11 numerical variables for clustering
car_data <- mtcars[, -which(names(mtcars) == "car")]


# Standardize each numerical variable
# Each variable will have mean 0 and standard deviation 1
car_scaled <- scale(car_data)


# Calculate Euclidean distances
car_dist <- dist(car_scaled, method = "euclidean")


# Perform hierarchical clustering using different linkage methods
hc_single <- hclust(car_dist, method = "single")

hc_complete <- hclust(car_dist, method = "complete")

hc_average <- hclust(car_dist, method = "average")


# Plot the three dendrograms
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

plot(
  hc_single,
  labels = car_names,
  main = "Single Linkage",
  xlab = "",
  sub = "",
  cex = 0.6
)

plot(

  labels = car_names,
  main = "Complete Linkage",
  xlab = "",
  sub = "",
  cex = 0.6
)

plot(
  hc_average,
  labels = car_names,
  main = "Average Linkage",
  xlab = "",
  sub = "",
  cex = 0.6
)
# Reset plotting layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

I chose complete linkage and three clusters because the complete linkage dendrogram showed three reasonably distinct groups. Complete linkage also produced relatively compact clusters compared with single linkage, which showed more of a chaining pattern.

The cluster means help describe the characteristics of the three groups. Cluster 1 consists of relatively high-performance cars. These cars have high average horsepower (198.8), relatively high displacement (223.4), and all have manual transmissions on average (am = 1). They also have the highest average number of gears (4.6) and carburetors (5.2).

Cluster 2 consists primarily of smaller and more fuel-efficient cars. This cluster has the highest average mpg (24.65), the lowest average displacement (131.65), the lowest average horsepower (91.33), and the lowest average weight (2.58). It also has the highest average value for vs, suggesting that most cars in this cluster have straight engines.

Cluster 3 consists of larger and heavier cars. These cars have the lowest average mpg (15.05), the highest average number of cylinders (8), the highest average displacement (357.62), and the highest average weight (4.10). This group also has relatively high horsepower and consists entirely of automatic-transmission cars on average (am = 0).

All in all, the clustering separates the cars into a relatively high-performance group, a smaller and more fuel-efficient group, and a larger, heavier, less fuel-efficient group. The dendrogram and the differences in the cluster means support choosing three clusters because these groups have distinct characteristics.

Standardizing the variables was important because the variables are measured on different numerical scales. Since hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance is affected by variable scale, variables with larger numerical scales could disproportionately influence the distance calculations. Thyerefore standardizing each variable to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1 gives all variables a more equal influence on the clustering.
